title: Hayes v. Seattle
facts: Respondent Michael Hayes filed suit seeking damages against the city of Seattle in the Superior Court for King County, alleging that the city had previously conditioned approval of his application for a building permit on a reduction in the size of the proposed development on arbitrary and capricious grounds in violation of Washington Revised Code §64.40.020. The trial court granted summary judgment to Hayes, concluding that the city had acted arbitrarily and capriciously and awarded Hayes damages. The city of Seattle appealed the trial court's decision, arguing that the statute of limitations had expired and that Hayes was barred by the doctrine of res judicata from seeking damages as the issue of whether the city had acted arbitrarily and capriciously had been decided in an earlier action commenced by Hayes that sought to reverse the city's initial denial of his application. The Washington Court of Appeals held that while Hayes's claim was time barred by the statute of limitations, he was nonetheless entitled to damages under federal law for deprivation of his civil rights. The city of Seattle appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Is Hayes's claim barred by the statute of limitations? If not, is it barred by the doctrine of res judicata? If not, did the city act arbitrarily and capriciously in conditioning Hayes's application upon a reduction in the size of his proposed development?
conclusions: Justice Alexander's opinion for the Court ruled that Hayes's action was not time barred as the statute of limitations did not begin to toll when Hayes had exhausted his administrative remedies but rather when the city took final action and actually issued its conditional land use permit, which had occurred only thirty days before Hayes filed suit. Furthermore, the Court held that Hayes's action was also not barred by the doctrine of res judicata as although the facts giving rise to Hayes's current action and the facts giving rise to Hayes's previous action were identical and the two actions could therefore have been joined, the burden of proof required to obtain a writ overturning the city council's decision to and the burden of proof required to obtain damages were sufficiently different that res judicata could not be invoked. Finally, the Court concluded that the city of Seattle had acted arbitrarily and capriciously in conditioning Hayes's application for a building permit upon a reduction in the size of the development as it had not specifically described the adverse environmental impacts that provided the basis for this decision and had not either outlined mitigation measures or specified why any such measures would be insufficient.

title: State of Washington v. McClendon
questions: Whether the double jeopardy clause of the United States Constitution bars prosecution for driving a vehicle while under the influence of intoxicants if the Department of Licensing has already issued a probationary license to the driver.

title: Washington State Legislature v. Lowry
questions: Whether the Governor may veto a subsection of a bill if that subsection repeals an entire section of an existing statute. Whether the Governor may veto a portion of an appropriations bill placing conditions on an appropriation, and if so, whether that action vetoes the appropriation itself.

title: Manor v. Nestle Food Co.
questions: Whether a parent company which is self-insured under the Industrial Insurance Act as to both itself and a subsidiary is immune from third-party liability for an industrial injury suffered by an employee of the subsidiary.

title: State of Washington v. Valentine
questions: Whether the trial court in this prosecution for assaulting a police officer properly instructed the jury that it is justifiable to resist an arrest only to prevent serious injury or death, and that the use of force to prevent an unlawful arrest which threatens only a loss of freedom is not reasonable.

title: State of Washington v. Williams
questions: Whether an administrative law judge's finding that a welfare recipient had not intentionally received overpayments collaterally estops the State from prosecuting the recipient for welfare fraud.

title: Leingang v. Pierce County Medical Bureau, Inc.
facts: Petitioner Dennis Leingang filed suit against his health insurance provider, the Pierce County Medical Bureau, seeking unpaid benefits and alleging that it had violated Washington's Consumer Protection Act (§19.86.020) by engaging in unfair and deceptive practices after it had invoked an exclusion clause in Leingang's insurance contract to deny him reimbursement for medical expenses incurred in an automobile accident that were covered by his automobile insurance. The trial court dismissed Leingang's claim, ruling that the exclusion was enforceable and not contrary to public policy. The Washington Court of Appeals reversed the trial court's decision after the Supreme Court of Washington had in the interim held that exclusions of the sort invoked by the Pierce County Medical Bureau violate public policy, ordering the contested benefits to be paid to Leingang and remanding the case to the trial court to resolve the Consumer Protection Act claim. The Pierce County Medical Bureau appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the Pierce County Medical Bureau engage in an unfair and deceptive practice by denying benefits pursuant to a clause subsequently declared to be in violation of public policy?
conclusions: Justice Guy's opinion for the Court held that the Pierce County Medical Bureau had not engaged in unfair and deceptive practices by invoking the exclusion clause in Leingang's policy as it had relied upon a reasonable interpretation of existing law in doing so. Although the Pierce County Medical Bureau had not requested a legal opinion from the Insurance Commissioner to determine whether its interpretation of the law was in fact reasonable, it was not legally required to do so by any statute or regulation.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Magula v. Benton Franklin Title Co.
questions: Whether termination of an at-will employee based solely on the misconduct of her spouse constitutes "marital status" discrimination prohibited by RCW 49.60.180.

title: Ino Ino, Inc. v. Bellevue
facts: Respondent Ino Ino, Inc. filed suit in the Superior Court for King County to challenge the constitutionality of the city of Bellevue's ordinance regulating adult cabarets. The ordinance regulated various aspects of the operations of adult cabarets, prohibiting physical contact between dancers and customers, prohibiting nude performances or graphic representations thereof outside of adult cabarets, and imposing a licensing requirement for the managers of adult cabarets that entailed a 14-day processing period. The trial court upheld the constitutionality of the ordinance. Ino Ino appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Do the provisions of the ordinance stipulating that a minimum distance be maintained between dancers and customers in order to prevent physical contact constitute a reasonable time, place, or manner restriction upon expressive speech? Are the provisions of the ordinance prohibiting displays or graphic representations of nudity outside of adult cabarets unconstitutionally overbroad? Does the 14-day period required to process adult cabaret managers' applications represent an unconstitutional prior restraint upon speech?
conclusions: Justice Madsen's opinion for the Court affirmed in part and reversed in part the trial court's decision. The Court ruled that although the Washington State Constitution's guarantee of the right to freedom of speech (Article 1 §5) offers broader protection than the First Amendment to the United States Constitution to expressive speech, the prohibition of physical contact between dancers and customers was nonetheless constitutional as it promoted the important state interest in curbing the illegal secondary effects associated with adult cabarets without denying dancers the ability to convey their erotic message. However, the Court held that the ordinance's prohibition of displays and representations of nudity outside of adult cabarets was overbroad as the display of artistic works featuring nudity could fall within its scope. The Court also concluded that requiring that prospective managers of adult cabarets wait 14 days while their applications are processed imposed an unconstitutional prior restraint upon speech as the ordinance included no provision for the granting of temporary licenses.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Burnet v. Spokane Ambulance
questions: Whether the trial court properly prohibited plaintiffs from discovering or presenting evidence on a claim of corporate negligence.

title: Center v. Pollution Control Hearings Board
questions: Whether pollution discharge permits, which by Department of Ecology regulation are categorically exempt from State Environmental Policy Act requirements, must nonetheless be reviewed under SEPA if they are shown to be major actions that may significantly affect the environment.

title: Honey v. Davis
questions: Whether a ground lessor who subordinates his interest in leased property to the interest of a tenant's construction lender becomes a surety and is entitled to reimbursement from the tenant when the lender forecloses on the property.

title: Nelson v. McClatchy Newpapers, Inc.
facts: Washington's Fair Campaign Practices Act forbids employers from discriminating against employees on the basis of their political views and/or activities. Petitioner Sandra Nelson was employed as a reporter by The News Tribune, which objected to her public role as a local political activist on grounds that it undermined the newspaper's appearance of objectivity. Nelson's refusal to cease her political activities ultimately led to her reassignment, prompting her to file suit in the Superior Court for Pierce County on the basis of an alleged violation of the Fair Campaign Practices Act. The Superior Court granted summary judgment to respondent McClatchy Newspapers, Inc., ruling that The News Tribune's right to freedom of the press shielded it from liability. Nelson appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does the Fair Campaign Practices Act bar employers from discriminating against employees for refusing to remain politically abstinent? If so, would applying the Fair Campaign Practices Act to The News Tribune violate the newspaper's right to freedom of the press under the 1st Amendment to the United States Constitution and Article I §5 of the Washington State Constitution?
conclusions: Justice Sanders' opinion for the Court held that while the plain meaning of the Fair Campaign Practices Act encompassed discriminatory action by employers of the sort engaged in by The News Tribune, applying the statute to newspapers violates their 1st Amendment rights. In particular, the Court concluded that the broad protection given to press outlets' editorial discretion encompasses decisions made by newspapers such as The News Tribune that are intended to preserve their editorial integrity and credibility.

title: Smoke v. City of Seattle
questions: Whether a party seeking damages under RCW 64.40.020 for an arbitrary or unlawful permit action must have exhausted any available administrative remedies.

title: Niece v. Elmview Group Home
questions: Whether a nursing home resident who was sexually abused by an employee of the home has a tort action against the home, either based on vicarious liability or for negligent supervision or care.

title: Department of Social & Health Services v. Olver
questions: Whether Washington's law permitting recovery of the cost of Medicaid benefits from the recipient's estate allows recovery for benefits provided before the law was enacted.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: City of Kennewick v. Benton County
questions: Whether the Tri-Cities Coliseum is exempt from Benton County property tax under the Washington Constitution when the City of Kennewick owns part of the Coliseum in a joint venture with a private corporation.

title: White v. State of Washington
questions: Whether a state nursing home employee who is transferred for reporting suspected patient abuse has a cause of action based on the public policy reasoning developed in wrongful discharge cases, or a cause of action under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 for interference with her free speech rights.

title: Malyon v. Pierce County
questions: Whether the Pierce County Sheriff Department's volunteer chaplaincy program violates either the establishment clause of the First Amendment of the United States Constitution or Article I, § 11 of the Washington Constitution.

title: State of Washington v. Brown
questions: Whether the death penalty was properly imposed in the State of Washington after a jury trial when the defendant confessed to police detectives in Palm Springs, California that he murdered a woman in Seattle, Washington and the confession was recorded in California without his knowledge.

title: Hillis v. Department of Ecology
questions: This is a direct review of a trial court's order which ordered the Department of Ecology to process the respondent's water rights applications, forbade the Department from conducting watershed assessments prior to decisions on all pending water rights applications, and invalidated decisions of the Department based on its failure to comply with formal rule-making procedures under the Administrative Procedure Act.

title: City of Seattle v. McCready
questions: Whether the trial court correctly denied defendants' claim for attorney fees following this court's decisions in earlier appeals in this litigation (see 123 Wn.2d 260 and 124 Wn.2d 300).

title: Seeley v. State of Washington
questions: Whether the classification of marijuana as a Schedule 1 substance which makes the substance illegal for all uses including medical use violates the Washington State Constitution?

title: Munns v. Martin
questions: Does a Walla Walla city ordinance and a SEPA regulation, requiring a waiting period before a church may demolish a church-owned building and replace it with a pastoral center on church property, burden the free excercise of religion in violation of the First Amendment and the Washington Constitution?

title: McIntyre v. Department of Health
questions: What is the proper standard of proof in medical desciplinary proceedings?

title: State of Washington v. Blank
questions: Indigent Defendant's who were permitted to appeal at public expense raise various challenges to the constitutionality of RCW 10.73.160, which allows an appellate court to issue an order requiring convicted indigent defendants to pay appellate costs including the fees for appointed counsel.

title: Washington State Coalition for the Homeless v. Department of Social & Health Services
questions: Whether the Department of Social and Health Services is obliged by constitution or statute to develop and implement a comprehensive plan to provide services to homeless children and their families.

title: Monroe v. Soliz
questions: Whether RCW 13.40.280, which allows the Department of Social and Health Services to administratively transfer dangerous juvenile offenders to an adult jail, violates the constitution.

title: State of Washington v. Virginia Warden
questions: Whether the jury can or should be instructed on manslaughter as a lesser included offense or a lesser degree offense of first or second degree murder in a trial.

title: Allstate Insurance v. Peasley
questions: Whether an exclusion in a homeowner's insurance policy for injuries resulting from "intentional or criminal acts of an insured" excludes coverage for injuries from conduct for which the insured was convicted of reckless endangerment.

title: State of Washington v. Berlin
questions: Whether the jury can or should be instructed on manslaughter as a lesser included offense or a lesser degree offense of first or second degree murder in a trial.

title: State of Washington v. Becker
questions: Prosecution for delivery of cocaine in a school zone. Delivery occurred in a downtown Seattle area near an office building housing an alternative education program run by the Seattle School District. The primary issue on appeal is what constitutes a school zone for sentence enhancement purposes.

title: State of Washington v. Rivard
questions: Whether the implied consent statute requiring a police officer to inform a driver of the right to refuse a blood alchohol test and the right to an additional independent blood test applies when the driver is not under arrest, but has been involved in a serious automobile accident.

title: State of Washington v. Groom
questions: Are police officers immune from prosecution for searches they reasonably believe are lawful?

title: In re Personal Restraint of Johnson
questions: After a defendant is convicted, and the law changes in a way that might reduce his 261-month sentence by 11 months, is he entitled to a new sentencing hearing even though he has already complained once about the length of his sentence?

title: Riss v. Angel
questions: Members of a homeowners association maintain that they properly rejected Plaintiffs' residential building plans under their subdivision's restrictive covenants, and that decisions by the trial court and the Court of Appeals to the contrary are in error.

title: Keene v. Edie
questions: Whether a tort victim, who has obtained a judgment against a married tort-feasor in the tort-feasor's individual capacity, may execute upon the tort-feasor's undivided one-half interest in community real property.

title: State of Washington v. Smith
questions: Whether the trial court's "to convict" jury instruction on conspiracy to commit murder properly listed the elements of that offense and, if not, whether the deficiency could be and was cured by other instructions.

title: State of Washington v. Walden
questions: Whether a jury instruction on the reasonable degree of force used in self-defense made the law manifestly apparent to the average juror?

title: State of Washington v. Miller
questions: Whether it is harmless error for the trial court to omit the element of delivery to a third party from a jury instruction defining the crime of conspiracy to deliver marijuana.

title: Amren v. City of Kalama
questions: Whether a State Patrol report submitted to the City of Kalama regarding an investigation of citizen complaints against the City's police chief is exempt from disclosure under RCW 41.06.450 and 42.17.295 which allows the destruction of information relating to state employee misconduct to be destroyed when it has been determined that the information is false and the employee has been exonerated of wrongdoing.

title: Kingery v. Department of Labor & Industries
questions: Can a widow presently seek benefits from the Department of Labor & Industries based on newly discovered evidence regarding the cause of her husband's on-the-job death, which occurred some eight years ago, where she failed to fully pursue her claim at that time?

title: Pasco Police Officers' Ass'n v. City of Pasco
questions: Whether management rights and hours of work clauses are mandatory subjects of bargaining upon which the employer could insist to impasse.

title: Louisiana-Pacific Corp., et al. v. ASARCO, Incorporated
questions: Whether a prevailing party under the private right of action of the Model Toxics Control Act is entitled to recover expanded costs of attorneys' fees and litigation expenses.

title: Greater Harbor 2000 v. City of Seattle
questions: Whether appellant Greater Harbor 2000, a group of non-abutting property owners in Seattle, has standing to challenge a decision by the City of Seattle to grant preliminary approval of a petition by the Port of Seattle to vacate 15.2 acres of public streets.

title: Department of Ecology v. Acquavella
questions: Whether the superior court correctly determined the amount and scope of the Yakima-Tieton Irrigation District's water right in the Yakima River Basin.

title: Wallace v. Evans
questions: Whether a motion to dismiss for want of prosecution may be granted where the case is noted for trial before the dismissal motion is heard, regardless of how long the plaintiff's action has been inactive.

title: State of Washington v. Stenson
questions: This is an appeal from a death sentence. The appellant's brief makes 33 assignments of error and states 41 issues. No attempt has been made to summarize those issues for this list.
